title: King Rastus Brown and the buck dance
summary: Green explains and demonstrates the buck dance, introduced by King Rastus Brown, a break with heel pushes and leaps like a bucking horse.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Tell me a little bit about King Rastus Brown at the Hoofer's Club. What was he like in the Hoofer's Club?
Well, King Rastus Brown introduced what they called buck dance, see. He was the originator of that, buck dance. You see?
What is a buck dance?

Well, now, I could get up and show you a demonstration and explain it also. As a tap dancer would be dancing, when he gets to the improvisation of the melody or song, there was what was known as a break, and he had in the buck dance, introducing this break, and that's where you would see the buck. It's like a deer, like a running deer. He runs so much, and then he would jump, you know, about three or four jumps and leaps like that. Well, each time this occurs in the buck dance, that's what he named it after. He named it buck dance because of that character in the dance.
It would be nice if you could show me that. Shall we do it?
Sure, certainly.
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
Did you see the bucks? I made about $15.00. (Laughter). Yeah, well that's the authentic buck dance, see, and King Rastus Brown, that's what he introduced
from the Hoofers Club fraternity.
(Recording interruption)
Chuck, is that used now, the way you were doing the buck dance? Do you use that now?
Yes. Twice.
Do you use it exactly as you've used it there, or have you changed it, or --
Well, I've given it what you call a more --
Embellished on it?
More equipment, yes. More installation in it. All the great, great dancers, tap dancers, featured a time step somewhere in their tap dance.
Because you say that was Dancing Dodson.
No. That was King Rastus Brown.
Oh, I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. Yes. But he does go -- he goes quite a way back, King Rastus.
King Rastus Brown does, yes, he goes quite a ways back.
So you say you do utilize that same buck dance in your dancing today. That's just a part of it.
Right. Every tap dancer, somewhere in their tap dance is the buck dance.
Uh-huh. It's a common dance used.

It's considered, you know, greatly artistic. That's why the -- what you call clogging, you know, waltz clogging, tap dance, that's how that was moved out, because of buck dancing, you see. Buck dancing became a favorite with other tap dancers. So they discontinued these dances like the strut, see, and clogging.
I would imagine it does, because it's very musical, and I see you were using your heels.
Yes.
Which most dancers find that difficult to do, even today.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, everytime he had something, he would say (Unintelligible). In buck dancing you touch the heel to begin what was known as the change, which is a break. After each step, the tap dancer demonstrated a tap break, and his tap, instead of using like the whole -- the ball of the foot or, you know, the toe and the heel of the foot, he would just use the heels. That was like a push. You call that pushing off, because he got the buck, to start the buck, like the jump or the leap, see, and it's like a buck, like in a rodeo, when the horse bucks, you see.
